intro.html: An argument has moves, and each move has a word. You make a claim (assert, contend, or, without proof, allege). Your opponent answers it (rebut) and may even prove it wrong (refute). Someone may give in on a point (concede). You can argue for a cause (advocate) and urge others to act (exhort). The whole art of persuading is rhetoric, and a fierce attack on an idea is a polemic.
The key difference: to rebut is to argue against a claim, whether or not you win; to refute is to prove it wrong. Saying “that’s not true” is neither: it is just a denial.

words.def: the art of persuasive speaking or writing; also, showy talk with little substance
words.ex: The debate coach taught {rhetoric}: how to open strong, use examples and end with a question.
words.ctx: The salesman’s pitch was all {rhetoric} and no facts: grand promises and stirring phrases, but not one word about the price or the warranty.
words.etym: From Greek rhetorike, “the art of the public speaker,” from rhetor (speaker).
words.note: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer: “Who doesn’t love a snow day?”

mn.cue: RHETOR = SPEAKER: the art of winning a crowd
mn.text: With a pause here and a question there, Jamal wins over the whole crowd using nothing but well-chosen words. He is a master of {rhetoric}.

scene.alt: A speaker at a podium wins over a cheering crowd with his words.

words.def: to state something firmly and confidently
words.ex: Zoe {asserted} that her cat could open doors, and then the cat did.
words.ctx: The author does not merely suggest that sleep helps memory; she {asserts} it plainly in the first sentence and spends the chapter backing it up.
words.etym: From Latin asserere, “to claim, declare”: ad (to) + serere (to join).

mn.cue: a SERGEANT doesn’t ask: he ASSERTS
mn.text: “We march at dawn!” the sergeant says, firm and sure, without a trace of doubt. He doesn’t ask; he {asserts}.

scene.alt: A man in a cap firmly announces the plan while two children salute.

words.def: to argue that something is true; also, to compete
words.ex: Maya {contends} that summer vacation should be a month longer.
words.ctx: Some historians {contend} that the bridge was built by the Romans, but others point out that its stones were cut with tools invented centuries later.
words.etym: From Latin contendere, “to strive, compete”: con (with) + tendere (to stretch).
words.note: Contend also means to compete (to contend for the title) or to struggle (to contend with bad weather).

mn.text: In the class debate, Maya argues hard that summer should be longer, and she has three reasons ready. She {contends} it.

scene.alt: Two teens at podiums argue opposite sides in a class debate.

words.def: to claim something, especially wrongdoing, without proof yet
words.ex: Pip {alleged} that his sister ate the last cupcake, but he had no proof.
words.ctx: The neighbors {allege} that the factory dumps waste into the creek at night, and they have asked the state to send inspectors to find out.
words.note: News reports say “the alleged thief” because no one has proved the charge yet.

mn.cue: a-LEDGE: out on a LEDGE with no proof
mn.text: Pip says his sister ate his cupcake, but he has nothing to back it up, only a guess. He is out on a ledge: he {alleges} it.

scene.alt: A boy points at his sister and claims she ate his cupcake, while she shrugs in confusion.

words.def: to prove that a claim is wrong
words.ex: Sami {refuted} Rex’s claim by showing him a photo of a real moon rock.
words.ctx: For years people believed the bridge was unsafe, but the engineer’s tests {refuted} that belief: it held three times the weight of the heaviest truck.
words.etym: From Latin refutare, “to drive back, disprove.”
words.note: To refute is to prove wrong, not just to deny or argue against.

mn.cue: RE-FUTE: PROOF puts the boot to it
mn.text: Rex claims the moon is made of cheese, so Sami shows him a moon rock in the science book. Sami {refutes} the claim: he proves it wrong.

scene.alt: A boy proves with a science book that the moon is rock, not cheese, while another looks shocked.

words.def: to argue against a claim by giving an answer
words.ex: Each speaker had two minutes to {rebut} the other side’s points.
words.ctx: The lawyer rose to {rebut} the witness, pointing out that the street lamp had been broken that night; whether the jury believed her was another matter.
words.etym: From Old French reboter, “to push back.”
words.note: To rebut is to answer an argument; it does not mean you won. Winning with proof is refute.

mn.text: Each time Maya makes a point, Dev bounces an answer right back, like a ball off a wall. He {rebuts} every claim, though he may not win.

scene.alt: Two debaters bounce points back and forth like a ball.

words.def: to admit that something is true, often unwillingly
words.ex: After the long chess game, Grandpa {conceded} that Kai had won.
words.ctx: Though she still disliked the plan, the team captain {conceded} that it would save time, and she agreed to try it for a week.
words.etym: From Latin concedere, “to give way, yield”: con + cedere (to go, yield).

mn.text: After a long chess game, Grandpa tips over his own king and smiles: “You win.” He {concedes}.

scene.alt: A grandfather smiles and admits defeat at chess while his grandson cheers.

words.def: to speak or argue in favor of
words.ex: Rosa {advocated} for a crosswalk in front of the school.
words.ctx: Doctors have long {advocated} washing hands before meals, explaining that this simple habit keeps many germs from spreading.
words.etym: From Latin advocare, “to call to one’s aid”: ad (to) + vocare (to call).
words.note: As a noun (AD-vuh-kit), an advocate is a person who speaks up for a cause or a person.

mn.cue: AD-VOC: add your VOICE for it
mn.text: Rosa adds her voice to the call for a crosswalk near the school, speaking up at every meeting. She {advocates} for it.

scene.alt: A teen calls out for a school crosswalk while a girl cheers beside a traffic cone.

words.ex: The coach {exhorted} her runners to give everything on the last lap.
words.ctx: The old captain {exhorted} the crew not to give up, reminding them that the harbor lights were only a few miles away.
words.etym: From Latin exhortari, “to encourage greatly”: ex (thoroughly) + hortari (to urge).

mn.text: On the last lap, the coach runs alongside the track, hollering, “Faster! You can do it!” She {exhorts} her runners.

scene.alt: A coach shouts encouragement as a runner speeds around the track.

words.def: a strong written or spoken attack on an idea
words.ex: His letter to the editor was a fiery {polemic} against the new parking rules.
words.ctx: The book is less a balanced history than a {polemic}: every chapter attacks the old king and ignores anything good he did.

mn.cue: POLE-MIC: grab the MIC and attack
mn.text: Victor grabs the mic and launches a fiery attack on the new school schedule, calling it the worst idea in history. His speech is a {polemic}.

scene.alt: A furious man with a microphone attacks the new school schedule.

head: move
word
rows: admit the other side is right

after.html: Test makers love refute. A writer who refutes a claim proves it false; a writer who merely rebuts or disputes it has only argued against it.

choices: The new fossil refuted the old theory: the animal had feathers after all.
He refuted the charge by shouting “No!” three times.
She refuted her friend’s idea because she did not like it.
The team refuted the game by forfeiting.
items.why: To refute is to prove wrong, and the fossil is proof. Shouting or disliking an idea is only denying it.

items.q: True or false: if you rebut an argument, you must have proved it false.
items.why: False. To rebut is to argue against, whether or not you win. Proving it false is refuting it.

items.q: Why do news reports say “the alleged thief”?
choices: The charge has not been proved yet.
items.why: To allege is to claim without proof yet; the person is only accused.

items.q: True or false: a candidate who concedes admits that the other side won.
items.why: True. To concede is to admit something, often unwillingly, such as defeat.
